Activation function, f(net) or f(w,x) is defined as
net = wixi 
f(net): 1 if net >= θ, -1 else (if net < θ)
Output a is either 1 or -1 chosen for binary class.
θ is a threshhold value.
Weight adjustment on the ith component (or feature) of the input vector, wi can be defined:
wi = l(t – a)xi, where l is a learning rate (0.0~1.0) to control the speed of convergence, t is the desired output value (class label) from the training set, a is the perceptron output value (e.g., either 1 or -1 in this case) for the current input case xi in a vector, Xn. wi will be used to adjust the weight of xi for the next input case, Xn+1. 
Perceptron algorithm learns the weight W from the training set by adjusting the weights to minimize the average error as follows:
If t = a, do nothing
Else (error), adjust the weight vector for the next case by Wn+1 = Wn + Wn
Repeat this process for all examples in the training set until converged (possibly reusing the training data).

Useful features of sigmoidal function:
S-shaped non-linear and continuous function in the range of 0 ~1
Differentiable (has a derivative) at each point and derivative calculation is easy.
The value of derivative is greatest where the sigmoidal function is changing most rapidly.

Sigmoidal activation function: f(net)=1/(1 + e-net), where net = wixi
The value of f(net) is continuous 0~1, not binary.
Output of f(x) is normalized to 0~1

Goal: Given training data, find a set of weights that fits outputs of neural net to desired classification.
Mechanism:
For each training example, propagate the inputs Forward for activation.
Backpropagate the error to previous layer and adjust the weights slowly in direction that reduces error.
Repeat this process until converged. (gradient descent approach).
Proven to converge on the nearest local minimum but
May not find the best weight setting. 
Sensitive to initial weight setting.
Works very slowly (long training time).
Many applications:
      solved many difficult real-world problems.

textBlocks:
How do we adjust weights for errors when using sigmoidal activation functions?
Use the delta rule (Rumelhart et al. 1986) for weight adjustment on the jth node from the ith input: wj =  l(tj – aj)f’(netj)xi where l is the learning rate, tj is the desired output, aj is the output of the node, and f’(netj) is the derivative of activation function, and xi is an input (= output from the previous node).

Concepts of the delta rule is shown in the following graph:

*l determines the size of learning step. 
*Learning algorithm uses gradient descent method to find the direction on this surface which most rapidly reduces the error (ending at a local minimum).
*Gradient is a measure of slope, as a function of direction from a point on a surface.
*This error surface represents cumulative error over a data set as a function of network weights.

Clustering tries to group a set of objects and find whether there is some relationship between the objects.

textBlocks:
The learning agent goes through trial-and-error, receives feedback or reward, and learns an optimal policy to accomplish goals within its environment.
Inspired by old behaviorist psychology, concerned with how an agent ought to take actions in an environment so as to maximize some notion of cumulative reward.
Reinforcement learning is most successful when the environment is big or cannot be precisely described. 
Unlike supervised learning, learning agent is not told directly what to do; rather, the agent discovers itself through exploration which actions offer the most reward.
Studied in many other disciplines, such as control theory, operations research (called approximate dynamic programming), information theory, simulation-based optimization.
In economics and game theory, reinforcement learning may be used to explain how equilibrium may arise under bounded rationality.
Supplemental material “Monte Carlo Tree Search and AlphaGo”, Monte Carlo Reinforcement Learning
slides.notes:
Game playing
- determining the best move to make in a game often depends on a number of different factors, hence the number of possible states that can exist in a particular game is usually very large. To cover this many states using a standard rule based approach would mean specifying an also large number of hard coded rules. RL cuts out the need to manually specify rules, agents learn simply by playing the game. For two player games such as backgammon, agents can be trained by playing against other human players or even other RL agents.
Control problems
- such as elevator scheduling. Again, it is not obvious what strategies would provide the best, most timely elevator service. For control problems such as this, RL agents can be left to learn in a simulated environment and eventually they will come up with good controlling policies. Some advantages of using RL for control problems is that an agent can be retrained easily to adapt to environment changes, and trained continuously while the system is online, improving performance all the time.

Use of domain knowledge in learning process
Cognitive scientist argue that learners learn better and faster based on the existing domain knowledge—knowledge is important in learning (although sounds counter-intuitive). 
Human can learn patterns by a few examples. 
Many machine learning algorithms such as ID3 and candidate elimination learn on the basis of regularities, similarities, or patterns in training data without using domain knowledge to guide generalization
Meta-DENDRAL as an Example (by Buchanan and Mitchel, 1978)
Knowledge is represented in the form of rules (use graphs of molecular structure for LHS and RHS)
Meta-DENDRAL infers the rules for the structure of organic molecules from their chemical formula and data. 
Explanations of the results are added after the inference as positive examples  for a rule
